theory.text: The queen works like a fence. Put it a knight's move away from the enemy king: from there it covers the rank and the file right next to the king without giving check, so the king's box shrinks. Each time the king steps back, follow it with the queen and keep that knight's-move distance. Rule of thumb: don't give checks. A check lets the king step out of the box, while a quiet queen move takes squares away for good.

moves.note: The queen goes to f4, a knight's move from the king on d5. Now the whole 4th rank is closed, and the king is stuck on the 5th rank and above.
The king stepped back to c6, so the queen follows to e5, again a knight's move away. The 5th rank is now closed as well.
On d5 the queen covers the whole 5th rank and the diagonal through c6 and b7.
The queen takes the 6th rank. The king only has the 7th and 8th ranks left.
The queen shadows the king to d6 and takes away c7.
The queen on e7 closes the 7th rank. The black king is trapped on the back rank and can only shuffle between b8 and c8.

theory.text: Once the king is stuck on the edge, stop moving the queen: its work is done. Walk your own king up the board. The enemy king can only shuffle along the edge while yours comes closer. The mate comes when your king guards the squares in front of the enemy king and the queen checks on the edge, either protected by your king or from far away.

moves.note: The queen on e7 holds the 7th rank, so the white king just walks. Black still has a8 and c8, so there is no stalemate.
The king heads straight for the b6 and c6 squares.
Each step brings the king closer. Notice that Black always keeps a free square on the back rank.
The king arrives on b6, guarding a7, b7 and c7.
The queen lands on c7, protected by the king on b6. It checks the king on c8 and covers b8 and d8. Checkmate.

theory.text: Stalemate is the only way to throw this ending away. If the enemy king has no legal move and is not in check, the game is a draw on the spot. The typical mistake is a queen move that takes the king's very last square without giving check. Near the corner, before every move, count the enemy king's squares: there must be at least one left.

moves.note: The king on a8 has only one square, a7. Playing Qb6 or Kb6 here would take a7 away without check, and that is stalemate. Instead the king steps to c7, which leaves a7 free.
Now the queen checks from b6, protected by the king on c7. Every square around a7 is covered: checkmate.

drills.hint: Start with Qf4 or Qg5 to fence the king in, keep the queen a knight's move away, then bring your king.
The queen can build the fence from far away. Then walk your king up the board.
The king is already in the corner. Keep it there with the queen, walk your king over, and count its squares every move.

lessons.title: Queen mate
lessons.summary: Fence the king in with the queen a knight's move away, walk your own king over, and never stalemate.

theory.text: The rook cuts the board in two: the enemy king can never cross the rank or file the rook stands on. Your job is to make that box smaller, one rank at a time, with the help of your king. Three rules decide every move. If the kings stand directly opposite each other with one square between them, give a check with the rook: the enemy king must step back. If the enemy king is a knight's move away from your king, make a waiting move with the rook along its line. Otherwise, bring your king closer.

moves.note: The kings on d4 and c6 are a knight's move apart, so White waits: the rook slides to g5 and still guards the 5th rank.
Black stepped into the opposition on d6, directly opposite the king on d4. That is the moment to check: the king is driven back to the 7th rank.
The white king follows, staying close.
A knight's move apart again, so another waiting move along the 6th rank.
The kings face each other on c5 and c7, so the rook checks on h7 and pushes the king to the back rank.
Now the white king steps up to d6.
The king on c8 is a knight's move from d6, so White waits once more with the rook.
Black tries to run to the corner; the white king follows along the 6th rank.
Now a8 and b8 are the only squares left, and Black must step into the opposition.
Kings opposite on b6 and b8, rook checks on the back rank: checkmate.

theory.text: Two typical mistakes. First, random checks: a check that does not come with the kings opposite just lets the king walk out of the box. Second, leaving the rook next to the enemy king. If the king attacks your rook, move it to the far side of the board along the same line, so it keeps cutting the king off.

drills.hint: First cut the king off with the rook on a rank or file, then bring your king closer.
Put the rook on the d-file or the 5th rank to start shrinking the box.
Cut the king off along the 2nd rank, then march your king up from h1.

lessons.title: Rook mate
lessons.summary: Cut the king off with the rook, use the opposition, make a waiting move when needed, then check on the edge.

theory.text: Two rooks mate on their own. One rook stops the king from coming back down a rank, the other gives check on the next rank up. Then they swap jobs, one rank at a time, like climbing a ladder, until the king is pushed onto the edge. If the enemy king walks up to attack a rook, don't panic: swing that rook to the far side of the board along its rank and carry on climbing.

moves.note: The rook on b3 closes the 3rd rank. Together with the rook on a2, the king on h4 can no longer come down the board.
The first step of the ladder: the rook checks on the 4th rank and the king must climb to the 5th.
The other rook checks on the 5th rank while the rook on a4 still guards the 4th.
Check on the 6th rank.
Check on the 7th rank, and the king is pushed to the back rank.
The king on c8 was attacking the rook on b7, so the rook runs to h7, as far away as possible, and still guards the 7th rank.
The other rook also moves away from the king and lines up on the g-file.
The rook checks on the back rank, the rook on h7 covers the 7th rank: checkmate.

drills.hint: One rook to the 4th rank, the other checks on the 5th, and climb.
Start the ladder on the 3rd and 4th ranks. Keep the rooks far from the king.
Close the 2nd rank first, then climb. If the king attacks a rook, swing it to the other side.

lessons.title: Two-rook ladder mate
lessons.summary: Two rooks climb the board like a ladder, one rank at a time. No king help needed.

theory.text: Two bishops standing next to each other cover two neighbouring diagonals, a wall the enemy king can't cross. Bring both bishops and your king to the centre first. Then use the wall and your king together to push the enemy king towards the edge, one diagonal at a time. Rule of thumb: keep the bishops away from the enemy king, a few squares back, where it can't attack them. They work just as well from a distance.

Any corner will do. Once the king is in the corner, your king stands a knight's move from the corner square, one bishop covers the escape square on the edge and the other gives the final check along the diagonal. Watch for stalemate here too: when the king is stuck in the corner with no checks, make sure it still has a square to go to.

moves.note: The dark-squared bishop jumps to h6 and takes f8 and g7. The bishop on d3 already covers h7, so the king on g8 has just one square left, h8.
The white king steps to g6. Black still has g8, so this is not stalemate.
The light-squared bishop checks from c4 along the diagonal to g8 and drives the king back into the corner.
The other bishop checks from g7, protected by the king on g6. The bishop on c4 covers g8 and the king covers h7: checkmate.

drills.hint: Bring the bishops to the centre first (Bd3 and Bf4), side by side, then use the king.
Keep the bishops side by side and out of reach of the enemy king.

lessons.title: Two bishops mate
lessons.summary: Bishops side by side make a diagonal wall. Push the king to the edge, then into any corner.

stages.title: Stage 1 · Basic checkmates
stages.intro: Every won endgame finishes here. Learn to mate with a queen, a rook, two rooks and two bishops quickly, by method rather than by luck, and without ever giving stalemate.

theory.text: Two kings standing on the same file with one square between them are in opposition. Kings can never step next to each other, so whoever has to move must give way and let the other king through. The side that just moved into this position "has the opposition". With a pawn behind your king you even have a spare tempo: a pawn move hands the move back to the defender, and the defender's king has to step aside.

moves.note: The kings face each other on e4 and e6. White doesn't want to move the king, so the pawn makes a waiting move to e3. Now Black has to give way.
Black stepped to d6, so the white king goes around the other side to f5. This is called outflanking.
The white king takes the opposition on e5, facing the king on e7.
Again Black gave way, so the white king walks forward to d6, in front of the pawn.
With the king on the 6th rank, the pawn simply walks up.
The king stays in front of its pawn and takes the opposition on e6.
Black gave way again. Now d7 guards the queening square e8.
The pawn promotes on e8, protected by the king on d7.

theory.text: The most important winning rule: if your king stands on the 6th rank in front of your pawn, you win, whoever is to move. The only exception is the rook pawn. Step to the side, keep the queening square covered, and push.

moves.note: White steps to the side and keeps e7 under control. If Black goes to f8, the king goes to d7 and the pawn runs.
Black took the opposition on d8, but now the pawn moves instead of the king.
The pawn reaches e7. The black king is forced away from the queening square.
The king guards e8.
The pawn queens on e8.

theory.text: When you defend, do the opposite. Stay in front of the pawn and take the opposition every time the attacking king comes close. The typical mistake comes at the very end: when the pawn reaches the 6th rank, go straight back to the square in front of it, not to the side. Then, when the pawn checks you on the 7th, you can take the opposition again and the only way to go on is stalemate.

moves.note: White tries to go around on c5.
Black answered by taking the opposition on c7. The pawn moves up instead.
The pawn reaches d6.
The key moment: Black went straight back to d8, directly in front of the pawn, not to c8 or e8.
Black takes the opposition on c8 again. Now the pawn has to check.
The king on d8 blocks the pawn. White can only play Kd6, which is stalemate, or give up the pawn. A draw.

drills.hint: King on the 6th in front of the pawn: step aside with Kd6 or Kf6, then push.
Get your king to e6, d6 or f6 in front of the pawn first, then push.
Come forward and stay in front of the pawn. Take the opposition whenever White's king approaches.
The kings are in opposition. Use the pawn as a spare tempo with d3, then go around.

lessons.title: The opposition
lessons.summary: When the kings face each other with one square between them, the side that does NOT have to move wins the fight.

theory.text: Every pawn has key squares. If the attacking king reaches one of them, the pawn queens no matter whose move it is, so you don't need to calculate. For a pawn on the 2nd, 3rd or 4th rank, the key squares are the three squares two ranks in front of it: for a pawn on f3 they are e5, f5 and g5. Once the pawn has crossed into the 5th rank, the squares one rank ahead count as well. So the plan is always the same: king first to a key square, pawn second.

moves.note: The key squares of the f3 pawn are e5, f5 and g5. The black king guards e5 and f5, but g5 is free, and the white king takes it at once.
With the king on a key square, the rest is technique. The king keeps marching in front of the pawn.
The king reaches the 6th rank.
Opposition again on f6 against f8.
Black gave way, so the king takes e7 and controls the queening square f8.
Now the pawn walks up, guarded by the king.
The pawn promotes on f8, protected by the king on e7.

theory.text: Rook pawns are different. If the defending king reaches the corner in front of the pawn, it's a draw: the attacking king can't drive it out, and pushing the pawn only ends in stalemate. Even with your king right next to the corner, an h-pawn can't win against a king on h8 or g8.

moves.note: The black king stays in the corner, moving between g8 and h8.
The pawn moves up, but the king on h8 can't be pushed away.
Now White has no way to make progress. Kh6 is stalemate, and any other king move lets Black's king out to take the pawn. A draw.

theory.text: Two typical mistakes. When attacking, players push the pawn first and the king second, so the defending king blocks it. Remember: the pawn can always wait, the king has to get in front. When defending against a rook pawn, players leave the corner to attack the pawn. Don't: as long as your king stays in the corner, the pawn can never promote.

drills.hint: Shuffle between g8 and h8 and never leave the corner.
The key squares of the c3 pawn are b5, c5 and d5. Get your king there before you push.
The key squares of the d2 pawn are c4, d4 and e4. Step onto one now, before the black king arrives.
Run to the corner in front of the h-pawn: h8 or the squares next to it.

lessons.title: Key squares and the rook pawn
lessons.summary: If your king reaches a key square, the pawn queens whoever is to move. With a rook pawn, the defender's corner is a fortress.

theory.text: Imagine a square with one side running from the pawn to its queening square. If the defending king is inside that square, or can step into it with its next move, it catches the pawn. If not, the pawn queens. For a pawn on a4, the square has the corners a4, a8, e8 and e4. A king on e5 or anywhere inside catches it.

moves.note: The square of the a4 pawn is a4, a8, e8 and e4. With one move the king steps from f7 into it on e7.
Every pawn move makes the square smaller, but the king moves into the new square too.
The king reaches b7 in time and takes the pawn next move.

theory.text: Two details. First, a pawn on its starting square can move two squares at once, so draw the square from the square it would reach after the double step: a pawn on a2 is counted as if it stood on a3. Second, count only if nothing blocks the defending king. Pieces or pawns in its path, or the attacking king standing in the way, can make the king too slow even inside the square.

moves.note: The pawn jumps two squares. Its square is now a4, a8, e8 and e4, and the black king on g5 can't step into it in one move.
The square shrinks to a5, a8, d8 and d5. The king on f5 is still outside.
The pawn queens one move before the king gets there.

drills.hint: Step into the square straight away: Ke7.
The black king is outside the square. Just run.
Use the double step: after a4 the king is outside the square.
Count the square as if the pawn were already on a3, and step inside it now.

lessons.title: The rule of the square
lessons.summary: Can the king catch the pawn? Draw the square and you know without calculating.

theory.text: The opposition also works at a distance. If the kings stand on the same file with three or five squares between them (an odd number), that is distant opposition, and again the side that does NOT have to move has it. Taking the distant opposition early means you can take the close opposition later. Counting trick: count the squares between the kings. Odd number, and it's the opponent's turn: you have the opposition.

moves.note: The kings are on e3 and e8. Black steps to e7, so there are now three squares between the kings, e4, e5 and e6. That is the distant opposition.
White tries to march up the d-file towards the key squares c5, d5 and e5.
Black answers by taking the close opposition on d6. The king on d4 can't go forward.
Wherever the white king goes, the black king mirrors it on the same file.

White uses the spare pawn move, but the black king just stays in front of the pawn. Without a key square, the pawn can't promote: a draw. Note that 1...Kf7 instead of 1...Ke7 would lose, because the white king reaches d5 or e5.

theory.text: When the kings face each other and you can't go forward, go around. Outflanking means stepping diagonally past the enemy king to the side. The defender must follow to keep the opposition, and that lets you take the opposition again one rank further up. Shouldering is the defender's version: put your king in the path of the enemy king, like a body check, so it has to take the long way around.

moves.note: The kings face each other on d4 and d6. White spends the spare pawn move, so Black must give way.
Black went left, so White outflanks on the right side, to e5. The king gets closer to the 6th rank.
The kings face each other again, now on d5 and d7, with Black to move.
White goes around once more and reaches c6, a key square of the pawn. The win is now certain.
The pawn steps to d7, protected by the king on c6.
The king takes control of d8, and the pawn queens next move.

drills.hint: Don't wait for the white king to come close. Step forward now so that you can take the opposition when it arrives.
The key squares of the d3 pawn are c5, d5 and e5. Walk towards them before the black king can oppose you.
Take the opposition with your king first. Keep the pawn back as a spare tempo for later.

lessons.title: Distant opposition and outflanking
lessons.summary: Kings far apart can still be in opposition. Count the squares between them, and learn to go around the enemy king.

theory.text: Sometimes a position is winning only if it's the opponent's move. You can't pass in chess, but a king can lose a move: it walks around a little triangle of three squares and is back on its starting square after three moves. Meanwhile the enemy king, which has only two good squares, has just shuttled back and forth. The same position appears again, but now with the opponent to move. This works when you have more room than the defender. Look for it when you are stuck in front of a blocked pawn chain.

moves.note: The king on d4 can't make progress directly, and c5 just trades pawns into a draw. White starts a triangle: d4, e4, d3, and back to d4.
Black uses the moment to attack the pawn on c4.
The second corner of the triangle protects c4.
The black king has to step back to b6. It only has these two squares.
White is back on d4 and Black is back on b6, but now it is Black's move. The triangle has passed the move.
Black has to let something go. If the king goes to a5, the pawn break c5 wins.
Now c5 is too far away for the black king, so the white king heads for d6 via f5.
The d6 pawn falls, and the d5 and c4 pawns will promote.

drills.hint: Walk the triangle d4, e4, d3, d4 to give Black the move.
The c4 pawn is attacked. Guard it with Kd3, then come back to d4 with Black to move.
The position with Black to move is lost for Black. Lose a tempo with your king, for example Ka5, Kb5, Ka6, and then go for d6.

lessons.title: Triangulation
lessons.summary: When you need to pass the move, walk your king around a triangle while the enemy king can only go back and forth.

theory.text: When pawns stand face to face and the enemy king is far away, a sacrifice can open a path for one pawn. In the classic breakthrough with pawns on a5, b5 and c5 against a7, b7 and c7, push the middle pawn first. Whatever Black takes with, a second sacrifice clears the way for the last pawn. Before you try it, count: the pawn that gets through needs three or four moves to promote, so the defending king must be at least that far away from the queening square.

moves.note: The middle pawn goes first. It attacks a7 and c7 and must be taken.
Black took with the c-pawn, so the a-pawn sacrifices itself on a6.
Now the c-pawn has a free run to c8. Black's pawns on a6 and b6 are too slow to matter.
The king on f7 was much too far away. White has a new queen.

theory.text: If Black captures the other way, you mirror the idea: take away the pawn that would stop yours, then run with the one that is left.

moves.note: This time Black takes with the a-pawn.
Now the c-pawn is the sacrifice. If Black ignores it, c6 takes on b7.
The a-pawn is free. Nothing stands on a7 or a8.
The a-pawn promotes on a8.

theory.text: The typical mistake is to start with an outside pawn. After 1.a6 bxa6 2.bxa6, or 1.c6 bxc6 2.bxc6, White has simply lost a pawn and the black king walks over and wins. Only the middle pawn attacks two pawns at once. The defender has a lesson too: if it is your move in this structure, play b6 first yourself and the breakthrough never happens.

drills.hint: Start with the middle pawn: b6. Then sacrifice the pawn that the black pawns can stop.
Same idea for Black, from the other side of the board: the middle pawn goes first with b3.
The breakthrough works on the kingside too. Which pawn attacks two black pawns at once?

lessons.title: Pawn breakthroughs
lessons.summary: Three pawns against three can break through. Sacrifice two pawns to queen the third.

theory.text: An outside passed pawn is a passed pawn far away from the other pawns, usually on the a- or h-file. It is often worth more than a whole extra pawn. Push it to decoy the enemy king. While the king runs after it, your own king walks to the other wing and eats the pawns there. Rule of thumb: in a king and pawn ending, the side with the outside passed pawn is usually winning, even when the material is equal.

moves.note: The a-pawn is far away from all the other pawns. White pushes it so the black king must go after it.
The black king reaches b7 in time to stop the pawn, but it is now far from its own pawns on f6 and g6.
Meanwhile the white king heads for the kingside.
The king attacks the pawn on f6.
Both black pawns are gone. White has two pawns left and the black king is on the other side of the board: an easy win.

theory.text: A protected passed pawn is a passed pawn defended by another pawn. The enemy king can never take it, so it must stay in front of it or near it forever. That leaves your king free to attack anywhere else. Rule of thumb: the defending king can't guard a protected passed pawn and its own pawns on the other wing at the same time.

moves.note: The b5 pawn is protected by the pawn on a4, so the king on c5 can't take it. White's king is free to go to the kingside.
The king attacks the pawn on g5.
The g5 pawn falls. Black's king can't go after the white king, because the moment it leaves the b5 pawn's square, b6 and b7 win.
Now White simply makes a new passed pawn on the kingside.
The g-pawn walks to g8 with its king next to it. Black is lost.

theory.text: The typical mistake is to rush the passed pawn to its queening square too early, or to trade it off. Its job is to pull the enemy king away. Keep it as a threat, push it only when the king has to follow, and use the time to win pawns with your king.

drills.hint: Push the a-pawn to pull the black king away, then march your king to the kingside pawns.
The b5 pawn is protected. Leave it there and go and win the g5 pawn with your king.
Black has the outside passed pawn on a5. Push it to decoy the white king, then attack g3 and h4 with your king.
Your a-pawn is the outside passer. First improve your king, then push the a-pawn when it pulls the white king away.

lessons.title: Outside and protected passed pawns
lessons.summary: A passed pawn far from the other pawns drags the enemy king away; a protected one ties it down. Either way, your king eats the pawns on the other side.

theory.text: On a chessboard, a diagonal path is exactly as long as a straight one. From h8 to h4 the king needs four moves going straight down, and also four moves going in a zigzag through g7, f6 and e5. So a king walking diagonally can chase two things at once. In Réti's famous study, the white king on h8 looks hopelessly behind the h-pawn, yet it gets close to its own c-pawn and into the square of the black pawn at the same time.

moves.note: The king heads down the long diagonal. It is outside the square of the h-pawn for now, but it also moves towards its own pawn on c6.
Two threats now: the king can help the c-pawn with Ke7, or chase the h-pawn.
Black stops the c-pawn by attacking it.
The king switches to the other goal. From e5 it is inside the square of the h-pawn.
Black took the c-pawn, but now the white king catches the h-pawn.
The h-pawn falls. A draw.

theory.text: What if Black ignores the c-pawn and just runs with the h-pawn? Then the white king supports its own pawn instead, and both sides queen.

moves.note: Black races with the h-pawn.
The king switches to the c-pawn and walks next to it.
The king on d7 protects c7 and c8.
Both sides have a queen. A draw.

theory.text: The typical mistake is to chase the pawn directly along the edge. 1.Kh7 would be a full move too slow. Whenever your king must go two places, look for a diagonal path that brings it closer to both.

drills.hint: Walk down the long diagonal: Kg7, Kf6, and keep both goals in reach.
The same study in a mirror. Your king goes down the diagonal through b7 and c6.
Now you are Black. Head up the diagonal through g2 and f3 towards both pawns.

lessons.title: The Réti manoeuvre
lessons.summary: A king walking diagonally can chase two goals at once: catch a pawn and support its own.

stages.title: Stage 2 · King and pawn endings
stages.intro: The most important endings in chess, because every other ending can turn into one. Opposition, key squares, the rule of the square, triangulation and passed pawns decide whether a pawn up is a win or only a draw. Here the king is a fighting piece: use it.

theory.text: The Lucena position: your pawn is on the 7th rank, your king stands right in front of it on the queening square, and the enemy king is cut off from the pawn by your rook. The pawn would queen at once if your king could step out, but every time it leaves, the enemy rook checks it from the side. The answer is to build a bridge. First, push the enemy king one more file away with a check. Then put your rook on the 4th rank. Your king walks out, and when the checks come close, the rook steps in between and blocks them.

moves.note: First the rook checks on d1 and pushes the black king one more file away from the pawn on b7.
This is the bridge. The rook goes to the 4th rank, where it will block the checks later.
The king steps out from b8, protecting the pawn's queening square from c7.
The king walks down towards the rook on d4.
The rook blocks the check on b4. Black has run out of checks, and the pawn promotes on b8.

theory.text: Why the 4th rank? Because the king needs to come down to the 5th rank to escape the checks, and the rook must stand one rank below it to block. If the rook is on the 5th or 6th, the king has no room. Two typical mistakes: walking the king out before the bridge is ready, so the checks never stop, and building the bridge while the enemy king is only one file away from the pawn. Then the rook trade on the 4th rank lets the king catch the pawn, so check it one more file away first.

moves.note: The black king on g7 is only one file away from the f-file. First the rook checks on g1 to push it to the h-file, so it can never get back to the pawn in time.
Now the bridge: the rook goes to g4 on the 4th rank.
The king leaves e8 and stays next to its pawn.
The black rook checks on the d-file, so the king steps to e6.
The king has reached the 5th rank, just above the rook on the 4th.
The rook slides from g4 to e4 and blocks the check. If Black takes on e4, the king takes back and the pawn queens, because the black king is too far away.

drills.hint: Rd1+ first, then Rd4 to build the bridge.
Push the black king one more file away with Rg1+, then build the bridge with Rg4.
Build the bridge on the 4th rank, then walk the king out and block the checks.

lessons.title: The Lucena position
lessons.summary: Win rook and pawn against rook by building a bridge for your king.

theory.text: The Philidor is the most important drawing method. Keep your king in front of the pawn, and put your rook on your 3rd rank, which is the 6th rank for Black. As long as the pawn stays on the 5th rank, the attacking king can't come forward to the 6th, because the rook would check it from the side. Just wait with the rook along that rank.

As soon as the pawn steps onto the 6th rank, the attacking king loses its shelter in front of the pawn. That is the signal: swing your rook to the far back rank and check the king from behind. It can't hide anywhere, and it can't protect the pawn and escape the checks at the same time. The typical mistake is to go to the back rank too early. With the rook passively on the 8th, the attacking king walks to the 6th rank and mates or queens.

moves.note: White puts the rook on the 7th rank. The black rook on a6 keeps the white king off the 6th rank.
Black just waits along the 6th rank. It doesn't matter which square.
Now the pawn advances to d6. The king on e5 can no longer hide in front of it.
The signal: the rook goes all the way back to b1, ready to check from behind.
White threatens mate on the back rank.
The checks begin.
If the king comes forward it is checked from below, and if it goes back to the pawn it is checked again.
The checks never end. A draw.

drills.hint: Keep the rook on the 6th rank until the pawn moves to d6, then go to the back rank.
The rook stays on the 6th rank. Only when the pawn reaches e6 does it go to the 1st rank.
Third-rank defence: the rook guards the 6th rank.
The pawn has reached d6 and White threatens mate. Start checking from behind at once.

lessons.title: The Philidor defence
lessons.summary: Hold rook and pawn against rook with the third-rank defence, then check from behind.

theory.text: The rook is at its best when it cuts the enemy king off. A rook on a file stops the king from crossing to the other side, so it can't reach the pawn. With the defending king cut off from the pawn by two files or more, the attacker usually wins easily: the king and pawn just walk up the board together. With the king cut off by only one file it depends on the details, and with the defending king in front of the pawn it is usually a draw.

moves.note: The rook on d1 keeps the black king on the queenside, far from the e-pawn. So the pawn simply runs.
The pawn reaches e7. Black's only hope is to check.
The king protects the pawn from f6.
The rook moves along the d-file to d8, guarding the queening square e8 and still cutting off the black king.
The king walks towards the black rook. On f4 it attacks the rook on g3, so the checks stop.
The pawn queens on e8.

theory.text: Cutting off works along ranks too. A rook on the 7th or 2nd rank traps a king on the edge, and a rook on the 5th or 4th rank keeps a king from coming down to stop a pawn. Rule of thumb: when your rook can choose between attacking a pawn and cutting the king off, cutting off is often stronger. The king is the best defender of all.

drills.hint: The black king is cut off along the d-file. Run with the pawn, and protect the queening square with your rook.
Keep the black king cut off along the d- or c-file, and bring king and pawn up together.
You are Black, and the white king is cut off along the d-file. Push the e-pawn and let your king escort it.

lessons.title: Cutting the king off
lessons.summary: A rook that cuts the defending king off from the pawn usually decides the game. Count the files.

theory.text: Tarrasch's rule: rooks belong behind passed pawns. Behind your own passed pawn, the rook pushes it forward and gets more active with every step the pawn takes. In front of the pawn, the rook gets more and more passive, because it has to stay there. If the enemy rook stands in front of your pawn, it is stuck there, and the enemy king must come over to help. Meanwhile your king is free to attack the pawns on the other side.

moves.note: The white rook on a1 is behind its pawn, and the black rook on a8 is in front of it. The pawn moves forward and the black rook has to stay passive.
The white king heads for the centre. It is free because its rook does all the work on the a-file.
The black king also comes over, but it has to stay near the a-pawn.
A waiting move. The rook stays behind the pawn.
Now White opens a second front on the kingside, where the black king can't help.
The white king walks into the black kingside pawns.
White has won a pawn and keeps the strong a-pawn. Black is lost.

theory.text: The same rule helps the defender. Put your rook behind the enemy passed pawn. Then the attacking rook has to stand in front of its own pawn, and the attacking king has to come over to support it, leaving its other pawns unguarded. Activity matters more than material in rook endings. A rook that attacks pawns and checks the king is often worth a whole pawn, while a passive rook stuck guarding loses slowly.

drills.hint: Your rook is behind the a-pawn. Push it, then march your king up while Black's pieces are tied down.
Your rook is behind White's a-pawn, which is right. Keep it there, keep your king near g7 and h7, and keep your pawns protected.
Same plan with a b-pawn: the rook on b1 is behind it, the black rook on b8 is stuck in front. Bring your king forward.

lessons.title: Rooks behind passed pawns
lessons.summary: The Tarrasch rule: put your rook behind the passed pawn, your own or the enemy's. An active rook is worth a pawn.

theory.text: Rook and a-pawn against rook is often a draw even with the pawn far advanced. The typical case: White's rook stands in front of its pawn on a8, the pawn is on a6, and the black king sits on g7 or h7, where the white rook can't leave a8 with check. The Vancura defence: put your rook on the 6th rank, on f6 or a similar square, so it attacks the pawn from the side. Now the white rook is tied to the pawn, and the white king has to walk over to protect it. But when the king arrives, there is nowhere to hide from the rook's checks from the side.

moves.note: The white king wants to come to b7 to support the pawn. The black rook on f6 attacks a6 from the side.
The black king simply waits on g7 and h7.
As soon as the king comes close, the checks begin from the side.
On b7 the king is checked along the 7th rank.
Even on b8 there is a check along the back rank.
The white king can't escape without abandoning the pawn. A draw.

theory.text: Two more details. If White pushes the pawn to a7, the black rook goes behind it on the a-file and the white king again finds no shelter. And keep your king on g7 or h7: there it stops the white rook from leaving a8 with a check or to cover the queening square. The typical mistake is a passive rook on the back rank or in front of the pawn: then the white king walks over, the rook leaves a8, and the pawn queens.

drills.hint: Keep the rook on the 6th rank attacking a6, and the king on g7 or h7. Check from the side when the white king comes close.
Bring your rook to the 6th rank to attack the a-pawn from the side, for example with Rb6.
The white king is close to its pawn. Start checking from the side, and come back to the 6th rank when the checks run out.

lessons.title: The Vancura defence
lessons.summary: Against a rook pawn with the rook in front of it, attack the pawn from the side and keep checking.

theory.text: The pawn divides the board into two sides. For an e-pawn, the f-, g- and h-files are the short side (three files) and the a- to d-files the long side (four files). When the defending king has to leave the pawn's file, it should go to the short side. The reason is the rook. Side checks only work from a distance: the rook needs at least three files between itself and the pawn, otherwise the attacking king simply walks up to it. With the king on the short side, the rook has the whole long side for its checks.

moves.note: White threatened mate with Rh8. The king steps to f8, the short side of the e-pawn.
White frees the king's path and threatens Kd7 or Ke7.
Now the rook checks from the long side, four files away from the e-pawn.
The king on d6 is checked again on the 6th rank.
If the king runs towards the rook, the checks go on along the ranks, and as soon as it leaves the pawn alone, the rook takes it.
The king can't escape the checks. A draw.

theory.text: Now see the mistake. With the king going to the long side, Black's rook has no room left, and White wins.

moves.note: The king goes to d8, the long side. That looks natural but loses.
The white king takes e7 at once. The black rook can't check from the side, because the only files on the short side, f, g and h, are too close to the pawn.
Black tries to stop the pawn from behind instead.
The king steps aside so the pawn can advance.
The king hides in front of its pawn. The black king is cut off on the long side, and White will win with e7 and a Lucena-type bridge.

drills.hint: White threatens Rh8 mate. Step to the short side, f8, and keep your rook far away on the long side for checks.
White threatens Rb8 mate. Check from the side at once with Rh6, and keep checking from a distance.
Your king is on the short side and your rook on the long side, exactly right. Check from the side whenever the white king approaches.

lessons.title: Short side and long side
lessons.summary: When your king is pushed off the pawn's file, send it to the short side and keep your rook on the long side for checks.

theory.text: A rook usually beats a lone pawn, but not always. The winning plan: stop the pawn with the rook, ideally from behind, and bring your king in front of the pawn. Once your king blocks it, the pawn falls. The defender's plan is to keep its king next to the pawn and push. Count the moves: if your king gets in front of the pawn first, you win; if the pawn reaches the 2nd or 7th rank with its king next to it while your king is far away, it is often a draw.

moves.note: The rook goes behind the pawn. Every square the pawn can reach is now covered.
The white king heads for the pawn. On e5 it already attacks d4.
The pawn falls, and it is a basic rook mate.
The rook cuts the black king off along the d-file.
Rook and king now push the king to the edge, exactly as in the rook mate lesson.

theory.text: A trick for the defender: shoulder the attacking king away with your own king, and when the pawn reaches the 2nd rank, the rook often has to give itself up for it. The typical mistake by the stronger side is to give lots of checks instead of bringing the king.

drills.hint: Put your rook behind the pawn on the d-file, then walk your king to it.
Your king is far away. Stop the pawn with the rook and bring the king as fast as you can.
Cut off the black king or stop the pawn from behind, then bring your king in front of the pawn.
Push the pawn with your king next to it. The white king is too far away to help.

lessons.title: Rook against pawn
lessons.summary: The rook wins if its king gets in front of the pawn in time. Otherwise, count the moves.

theory.text: Two connected passed pawns are very strong. If both reach the 6th rank and the enemy king is far away, they beat a rook without any help: when one pawn reaches the 7th, the rook can stop only one of them. Rule of thumb: with the pawns on the 6th the pawns win; further back, the rook and king usually win if the king is close. Push the pawn that the rook is not attacking.

moves.note: The g-pawn reaches the 7th rank and attacks h8.
The rook has to block on g8.
The rook is stuck. If it ever takes on g7, the f-pawn runs to f8, so White can bring the king first.
The king comes to support the pawns.
Next comes f7, attacking the rook on g8, and one of the pawns will queen.

drills.hint: Push g7 to tie the rook down, then bring your king or play f7.
Two pawns on the 3rd rank for Black, with the white king far away. Push the pawn the rook does not attack.
This time the pawns are far back and your king is close. Attack them with rook and king together.

lessons.title: Two connected pawns against a rook
lessons.summary: Two connected passed pawns on the 6th rank beat a rook on their own.

stages.title: Stage 3 · Rook endgames
stages.intro: Half of all endgames are rook endgames, and most of them are decided by a handful of known positions and rules. Learn how to win with Lucena, how to draw with Philidor and Vancura, where the defending king and rook belong, and why the rook goes behind the passed pawn.

theory.text: With a bishop and a rook pawn against a lone king, look at the colour of the queening square. If the bishop can control it, everything is fine. If it can't, it is the "wrong bishop", and once the defending king reaches the corner it is a draw: the king can't be driven out, and every attempt ends in stalemate. For an h-pawn, h8 is a dark square, so a light-squared bishop is the wrong one. For an a-pawn, a8 is light, so a dark-squared bishop is wrong.

moves.note: The pawn queens on h8, a dark square, and White's bishop is light-squared. So Black heads for the corner at once.
The king reaches g7, next to the corner.
The king is in the corner on h8. The light-squared bishop can never attack it there.
White can only push the pawn to h7 and give stalemate. A draw.

theory.text: The typical mistake for the defender is to leave the corner to chase the pawn or the bishop. Stay on h8, g8 and the squares next to them, and never let the enemy king take g7 and g8 away from you while you are not in the corner. With the right bishop, by contrast, the attacker wins easily: the bishop drives the king out of the corner.

drills.hint: Stay on h8 and g8. Never leave the corner.
The light-squared bishop can't control h8. Run with your king to the corner.
Here the bishop is dark-squared, the right one. Use it to drive the king out of the corner, then push the pawn.

lessons.title: The wrong rook-pawn bishop
lessons.summary: A bishop that can't cover the queening square can't win with a rook pawn. Run to the corner.

theory.text: When each side has one bishop and they run on different colours, the defender has a superpower: the attacker's bishop can never challenge the squares the defending bishop and king control. Even two pawns up, the attacker often can't break through. The defender's fortress: put your king in front of one pawn on a square of your own bishop's colour, where the enemy bishop can never chase it away, and let your bishop stop the other pawn from a distance along its diagonal.

moves.note: White is two pawns up, but Black's dark-squared bishop and king can build a wall. The king goes to d6, a dark square that White's light-squared bishop can never attack.
The bishop heads for the long diagonal from h8 to a1, where it will control e5 and d4.
From f6 the bishop covers e5 and d4.
White has set up the pawns on d4 and e4, but they can't move: d5 is covered by the black king, and e5 by both the king and the bishop.
Black just moves the bishop back and forth along the diagonal. White can never break through. A draw.

theory.text: The winning rule: two passed pawns win when they are far apart, about three files or more. The defending king can stop only one pawn and the bishop can't hold the other on its own, because the attacking king helps it forward on the bishop's other colour. Pawns close together, like the connected d- and e-pawns above, are usually a draw if the defender blockades them on the right colour.

moves.note: The pawns on b4 and g4 are five files apart. The white king goes to support the g-pawn.
The b-pawn advances on its own, protected by the bishop.
The black bishop stops the b-pawn on b7, but now it is busy there.
The white king walks around the black king to the g-pawn.
The g-pawn advances with check. The black king and bishop are overloaded, and White wins.

drills.hint: Blockade on the dark squares: king on d6 or e5, bishop on the long diagonal guarding d4 and e5.
The pawns are far apart. Push one, and use your king to support the other.
Two passed pawns five files apart. Bring your king to the g-pawn and let the b-pawn tie down the black king.

lessons.title: Opposite-coloured bishops
lessons.summary: With bishops on different colours, even two extra pawns often draw. But pawns far apart can win.

theory.text: A bishop is bad when its own pawns are fixed on its colour: it can only defend them, and it can't control the squares in front of them. It is good when its pawns stand on the other colour, so it can attack. Rule of thumb: put your pawns on the opposite colour of your bishop, and fix the enemy's pawns on the colour of their bishop.
In a good bishop against bad bishop ending, the winning plan is to tie the bad bishop to its pawns, then bring your king in. Sooner or later the defender runs out of moves: a zugzwang.

moves.note: All black pawns stand on light squares, like Black's bishop. The white bishop on e2 attacks b5 and h5, and the bishop on e8 has to defend both.
The white king walks in on the dark squares, which the black bishop can't touch.
The bishop can't guard everything any more. The b5 pawn falls.
And the d5 pawn falls too. White is winning easily.
The b- and d-pawns will now march up.

drills.hint: Your bishop attacks b5 and h5. Walk your king in on the dark squares, towards e5 and f4.
Bring your king to e5 via e3 and f4. The black bishop is busy defending b5 and h5.
First put your bishop on e2 to attack the pawns, then march your king to g5 or e5.

lessons.title: Good and bad bishops
lessons.summary: A bishop blocked by its own pawns is bad. Put your pawns on the other colour and attack the weaknesses.

theory.text: A knight is a short-range piece. It stops a passed pawn best by standing directly in front of it, or on a square that controls the queening square, with its king coming to help. Once a knight blocks a pawn, it is very hard to drive it away. Its weakness is distance. A knight needs several moves to cross the board, and it can't lose a tempo. Rook pawns are the worst: in the corner the knight has only two squares to work with.

moves.note: The knight from f1 heads for b1, the queening square. On d2 it already controls b1.
The black king attacks the knight.
The knight jumps to b1 with check and blocks the pawn.
The knight is attacked again, so it checks and comes back.
The knight returns to b1. Black can never get rid of it, and the white king comes later. A draw.

theory.text: A pawn beats a knight when the knight is too far away. Count the moves: if the knight can't reach a square in front of the pawn or control its queening square in time, push. Rule of thumb: a pawn on the 7th rank supported by its king usually beats a lone knight, and a rook pawn is the hardest pawn for a knight to stop.

drills.hint: Bring the knight to the queening square b1 or to a square that controls it, such as d2.
The knight is far away from a8. Make sure your new queen can't be forked, then promote.
Your a-pawn is one step from queening, and the knight on g8 is far away. Push.

lessons.title: Knight against pawns
lessons.summary: A knight stops a pawn best from in front, but it struggles against rook pawns and far-advanced pawns.

stages.title: Stage 4 · Bishops and knights
stages.intro: Minor-piece endings are about colours and distances. Learn when a bishop can't win, why opposite-coloured bishops draw so often, what makes a bishop good or bad, and how knights fight against passed pawns.

theory.text: You can only mate in a corner the bishop controls: with a light-squared bishop that means a8 or h1, with a dark-squared bishop a1 or h8. Bring all three pieces to the centre first, then push the enemy king to the edge. If the king runs to the wrong corner, drive it along the edge to the right one with the W manoeuvre: the knight hops in a W pattern while the bishop and king keep the king on the edge.
The final mate needs teamwork. Your king stands a knight's move from the corner, the bishop takes away the squares on its colour, and the knight covers the rest and gives the last check.

moves.note: The light-squared bishop takes b7 and c8 away. The black king can only go between a8 and b8.
The knight starts its journey towards a6 and c6.
From c5 the knight covers a6, b7 and d7.
The bishop checks from b7 and drives the king back to b8.
The knight checks from a6. The bishop covers a8 and c8, and the king on b6 covers a7, b7 and c7. Checkmate.

theory.text: Be patient. It can take up to 33 moves, and every move should take a square away from the enemy king. The typical mistake is to chase the king with checks; quiet moves that build the net work far better.

drills.hint: Centralise everything first, then force the king to the edge. The light-squared bishop means a8 or h1 is the mating corner.
The king is in the dark corner h8, but your bishop is light-squared. Drive it along the edge towards h1 or a8.

lessons.title: Bishop and knight mate
lessons.summary: The hardest basic mate: drive the king to a corner of your bishop's colour.

theory.text: A pawn on the 7th rank supported by its king still loses to a queen if it is a centre pawn or a knight pawn. The plan: use checks and pins to force the king to stand in front of its own pawn. While the pawn is blocked by its own king, you have one free move, and you use it to bring your king one step closer. Repeat the pattern until your king arrives, then win the pawn or mate.

moves.note: The queen checks from a1 along the 1st rank.
Another check, this time on the d-file.
A quiet move: the queen attacks e2 and covers e1. Black must defend the pawn.
Check from d3.
The king is forced in front of its own pawn on e1. Now the pawn can't queen.
The free move: the white king steps closer.
The queen pins the pawn and covers e1 again.
Again the king is in front of its pawn.
Another step closer. White repeats this until the king arrives.

drills.hint: Check or pin until the king blocks its own pawn, then step your king closer.
A knight pawn on b2 also loses. Force the king to b1 in front of it, then bring your king.
You are Black with the queen. Force the white king onto b8 in front of its pawn, then bring your king.

lessons.title: Queen against a pawn on the 7th
lessons.summary: Checks and pins force the king in front of its own pawn. Each time, your king steps closer.

theory.text: The staircase method fails against a rook pawn. When the defending king goes into the corner in front of its a-pawn, the attacker never gets a free move: any move that isn't check leaves the king with no moves at all, and that is stalemate.

moves.note: The black king protects the a-pawn and threatens to queen.
The queen attacks the pawn on a2 from a3, and Black protects it with the king again.
The king goes into the corner, right in front of its pawn. White has no free move: anything except a check leaves Black stalemated, and the white king on g1 is much too far away. A draw.

theory.text: Against a bishop pawn the defender has a different trick. The king runs into the corner, and if the queen takes the pawn, it is stalemate.

moves.note: The king leaves the pawn on c2 unprotected on purpose and goes into the corner.
If White takes the pawn with Qxc2, Black has no moves: stalemate.
The same position again. White can't make progress. A draw.

theory.text: These draws only work when the attacking king is far away. If it is close enough to join the attack, the queen wins, because it can get the free move it needs.

moves.note: The queen checks from f2.
The white king is close enough to come to b3 at once. There is no stalemate because the black pawn can still move.
Checkmate on e1. The king on b3 covers a2, b2 and c2.

drills.hint: Protect the pawn and head for the corner a1. When you're in front of your own pawn, White has no free move.
Go into the corner with Ka1. If the queen takes c2, it's stalemate.
Your king is close. Check once, then bring the king to b3.
Bishop pawn, but your king is near. Check from d4 and walk your king in.

lessons.title: Rook and bishop pawns against a queen
lessons.summary: A rook pawn or bishop pawn on the 7th can draw against a queen through stalemate, unless the attacking king is close.

stages.title: Stage 5 · Advanced endings
stages.intro: The hard ones: the bishop and knight mate, the queen against a pawn on the 7th, and the stalemate tricks that save rook and bishop pawns.
